papers.title: A Probabilistic Extension of the Division Property: Integral Distinguishers with Key-Independent Bounds
papers.abstract: Classical integral cryptanalysis relies on zero-sum properties that, for every key, hold with probability one. Existing arguments against such deterministic integrals, based on the division property and its algebraic variants, only exclude this extreme case: once the zero-sum probability falls below one, they say nothing about its actual value, nor about a probabilistic bias that could still be exploited. We develop a tool combining MILP-based trail search with a recursive evaluation of assignments to the constant inputs. It estimates the probability that no valid trail remains and uses an additional heuristic to predict the zero-sum probability. Applying this tool to PRESENT and GIFT, we obtain probabilistic integral distinguishers for 6 to 9 rounds, including 6- and 7-round PRESENT distinguishers using $2^4$ and $2^{12}$ plaintexts per structure, respectively. For the ASCON permutation, we obtain 4- and 5-round distinguishers using as few as $2$ and $2^{12}$ inputs per structure. We further explain algebraically the large bias of the 6-round PRESENT distinguisher, showing how the S-box and bit permutation restrict the way active variables combine. Finally, we show how these distinguishers can be used for key recovery, reducing both the data and time complexities compared to their deterministic variants for PRESENT and GIFT-64.

papers.title: SoK: Design-Level Backdoors in Block Ciphers Constructions, Detection, and Key Recovery
papers.abstract:
A block cipher is trusted once it resists every published attack and its
S-boxes pass the standard tests. A design-level backdoor turns this trust
against its users. Its designer hides a structure that only they can
exploit, and that the usual tests miss.

Four such backdoors have been published, by Rijmen and Preneel, Paterson,
Bannier and Filiol, and Peyrin and Wang. Each paper shows what the hidden
structure gives its designer. Everyone else needs answers to two other
questions. Does the structure also weaken the cipher against ordinary
cryptanalysis? Can an evaluator who holds only the specification find it?
Neither has been answered for all four designs, so an S-box that passes
the usual tests is trusted by default.

In this paper we answer both questions. We place the four designs in one
taxonomy and in Beyne's correlation-matrix framework. We give an algorithm
that recovers a partition trapdoor from the S-box tables, and prove that it
never reports a false one and, below an explicit cap, never misses one. We
show that inversion and affine equivalence preserve a trapdoor, while
extended affine and CCZ equivalence can erase it. We then attack KG-DES
(Paterson's S-boxes in DES), BEA-1 and LowMC-M.

The answer to the first question depends on the rest of the cipher. In
KG-DES the trapdoor makes ordinary attacks far stronger. The best
$16$-round differential characteristic has probability $2^{-21.23}$,
against $2^{-61.97}$ for DES, and a two-stage attack recovers the $56$-bit
key in minutes. In BEA-1 the trapdoor opens no useful trail. However, for
every key both ciphers act as an exact smaller cipher on the cosets, and
fall to known-plaintext distinguishers from about $2^{16.5}$ and
$2^{20.5}$ texts. An independent MILP model confirms every optimum it can
prove, and shows that single characteristics put the KG-DES boomerang at
$2^{-36.79}$ when it returns with probability $1$.

The answer to the second question depends on where the backdoor sits. Our
algorithm finds Paterson's trapdoor and BEA-1's four in the S-boxes that
carry them. Rijmen and Preneel's trapdoor needs unbalanced S-boxes, which
linear algebra exposes. LowMC-M's MALICIOUS backdoor sits in the linear
layers instead. With an ideal XOF a backdoored instance is distributed as
an honest one, so no test of the primitive finds it. Its holder recovered
the key from $35$ to $409$ queries in seven full-size measurements.

A deterministic trapdoor in the S-boxes therefore leaves a trace that a
sound algorithm finds. A trapdoor in unexplained linear layers leaves none,
and only constants derived verifiably from a public seed rule it out. We
recommend both as routine checks. Probabilistic trapdoors and trapdoors in
only some S-boxes remain open.

papers.title: Linear Cryptanalysis of TFHE-Friendly Cipher FRAST in the Average Key Setting
papers.abstract:
In the average key setting, a linear attack of Bak et al. on the TFHE-friendly stream cipher FRAST let wrong guesses pass, which they left as an open problem. The S-boxes of FRAST are public and random for every keystream block. For the mask on the least significant bit, we show that key differences fall into five indistinguishable classes per round. The filter of Bak et al. gives some wrong classes of the right parity a nonzero expected score. We compute the trail correlation exactly through the real cipher and bound the success of our statistic for every fixed master key. We bound its false alarms for a fixed master key with the last round kept and no filter, and for every attack against an ideal keystream.

With known XOF inputs, our algorithm Contract recovered the classes of a branch pair of 15 rounds and the master key of ten rounds. A cost model gives class recovery for every sampled key at 26 rounds with known inputs and for a third at 38 rounds with chosen inputs. In the accounting of Bak et al., it reaches full FRAST on weak master keys of density $2^{-11.8}$ to $2^{-5.4}$ within the claimed security. A distinguisher of full FRAST has a proved advantage on these keys, and its time over the advantage stays below the claimed security as well. Independent branch S-boxes remove the cheap classes at a cost in TFHE.

papers.title: Quantum Cryptanalysis on Two Feistel-Type Constructions
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of quantum computing, the security of traditional cryptographic systems is facing significant challenges. As a fundamental component of symmetric cryptography, block ciphers have attracted increasing attention regarding their quantum security in recent years. In this paper, we propose new quantum attacks on two Feistel-type constructions, i.e., New Structure IV and the lightweight block cipher LBlock, under the quantum chosen-plaintext attack (qCPA) model. First, we construct an 8-round quantum distinguisher for New Structure IV and perform an $r(r>12)$-round quantum key-recovery attack. Compared with Li et al.'s qCPA-based result presented at INSCRYPT 2024, our attack reduces the time complexity by a factor of $2^{n/2}$, where $n$ denotes the subkey length. Second, we design a 9-round quantum distinguisher for LBlock and extend it to an $r(r>15)$-round quantum key-recovery attack. The proposed quantum distinguisher covers one more round than Liu et al.'s automated-search distinguisher at ASIACRYPT 2025, which results in a $2^{16}$ reduction in the time complexity of our $r$-round quantum key-recovery attack on LBlock. Furthermore, by analyzing the structure of the round function and the key scheduling of LBlock, we reduce the subkey guess space for the 15-round attack from 76 bits to 52 bits, lowering the time complexity from \(O(2^{38})\) to \(O(2^{26})\) by a factor of \(2^{12}\).

papers.title: Cryptanalysis and Repair of "Decentralized Multi-authority ABE for NC$^1$ from BDH"
papers.abstract: We present a plaintext-recovery attack on the decentralized multi-authority attribute-based encryption construction of Datta, Komargodski, and Waters (Journal of Cryptology, 2023). The attack succeeds in the claimed static model with one corrupt authority and two users whose individual attribute sets remain unauthorized even when combined with the corrupt authority's attribute. The flaw is an incorrect extension of LSSS matrix-normalization invariance from complete secret shares to coordinate-wise ciphertext masks. A corrupt authority can expose these masks and remove identity binding from other users' decryption shares. We replace the coordinate-wise masks with independent full linear sharings of zero and prove static security under decisional bilinear Diffie-Hellman (DBDH) in the random oracle model. The repair retains the original matrix-width and row-labeling restrictions and leaves authority keys, user keys, decryption, and ciphertext size unchanged, while increasing encryption randomness and field arithmetic. We also give analogous attacks on both multi-authority attribute-based inner-product functional encryption constructions of Datta and Pal (PKC, 2023). The same modification restores correctness and matrix-substitution invariance for both variants. We prove static security of the repaired small-universe variant under asymmetric DBDH. For the large-universe variant, we identify a separate missing source-group encoding in the original reduction, formulate an augmented $L$-DBDH assumption, prove its hardness in the asymmetric generic bilinear group model, and give a static security reduction for the repaired scheme.
